questions.stem: When is a voltage induced in a straight conductor?

options.text: when it moves through a magnetic field
options.explanation: Relative motion between conductor and field induces the voltage.

options.text: whenever it is near a magnet, moving or not
options.explanation: Proximity alone induces nothing.

options.text: only when connected to a battery
options.explanation: Induction GENERATES voltage — no battery needed.

options.text: only when the field is switched off
options.explanation: The field is required, not removed.

questions.stem: A wire is held still in a steady, unchanging magnetic field. The induced voltage is:

options.explanation: Field strength alone is not a voltage.
No relative change means no induction.
A steady field through a still wire induces nothing.
Nothing changes, so nothing alternates.

questions.stem: The field through a stationary conductor is changed by pushing a magnet towards it. What happens?

options.text: the coil becomes a permanent magnet
options.explanation: The coil gains an induced voltage, not permanent magnetism.
Inducing does not demagnetise the magnet.

options.text: a voltage is induced because the field through the coil changes
options.explanation: The changing field is the induction trigger.

options.text: nothing — the coil must move instead
options.explanation: Either side moving induces; relative change is what counts.

questions.stem: The same wire is swept through the same field twice as fast. The induced voltage:

options.explanation: That inverts the speed link.
Speed is a size factor for induction.
Same sweep direction gives the same polarity.
Induced voltage grows with the speed of cutting.

questions.stem: Which change DECREASES the induced voltage in a moving wire?

options.text: sweeping through a weaker magnetic field
options.explanation: Field strength is a size factor — weaker field, smaller voltage.

options.text: sweeping faster through the same field
options.explanation: Faster sweeping increases the voltage.
A stronger magnet increases the voltage.

options.text: adding more turns to the coil
options.explanation: More turns increase the coil's induced voltage.

questions.stem: State the two ways a conductor or coil can have a voltage induced in it.
questions.modelAnswer: It moves through a magnetic field, or the magnetic field through it changes.

questions.stem: State three factors that affect the size of an induced voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: The speed of movement, the strength of the magnetic field, and the number of turns on the coil.

questions.stem: Explain why a wire carried ALONG the field lines, never cutting them, induces no voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: Induction depends on cutting across the field lines: the induced voltage arises from the relative sweeping of conductor through field. A wire that slides parallel to the lines never crosses any of them, so there is no cutting, no change in the field through the wire, and no induced voltage.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is held still inside a large coil while the coil is slid rapidly sideways past it. State whether a voltage appears and justify the answer.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes — a voltage appears. Induction needs relative change between coil and field: with the magnet still and the coil moving, the field threading the coil changes as the coil slides, which is one of the two induction triggers, so an induced voltage shows on the meter.

questions.stem: What does the meter show while a wire sweeps steadily through a field?

options.explanation: Steady sweeping gives a steady reading.

options.text: a steady deflection to one side
options.explanation: Constant cutting speed gives a constant induced voltage.
The deflection matches the cutting rate, not infinity.
Motion across the lines induces a real voltage.

questions.stem: The wire sweep is reversed. The meter needle:

options.explanation: Reversed motion still induces.
One reversal gives one opposite deflection.
Polarity follows the sweep direction.
Direction, not size, changes with reversal.

questions.stem: The wire stops mid-gap, still inside the field. The meter reads:

options.text: the same deflection as during the sweep
options.explanation: The kick dies when the motion stops.
Stopping removes the induction entirely.
No motion means no direction to reverse.

options.text: zero — no cutting, no induced voltage
options.explanation: Motion is required for induction here.

questions.stem: The sweep speed is doubled with everything else fixed. The deflection:

options.explanation: Faster cutting induces a bigger voltage.
That inverts the speed link.
Same direction of sweep, same side of deflection.
Size tracks the cutting speed.

questions.stem: Which change makes the meter kick REVERSE without touching the wire?

options.explanation: Cosmetics do not touch the physics.
Field reversal flips the induced polarity.
Length changes size, not polarity.
Speed changes size, not direction.

questions.stem: State what the wire does to the field lines in this setup.
questions.modelAnswer: The wire cuts across the field lines as it sweeps through the gap.

questions.stem: State the meter reading when the wire is held motionless between the poles.
questions.modelAnswer: The meter reads zero because no field lines are being cut.

questions.stem: Explain why the needle kick is only momentary if the wire is given one short push.
questions.modelAnswer: The push moves the wire for only a moment, so field lines are cut for only that moment. Induced voltage exists while cutting happens; once the wire settles, the cutting stops, the induced voltage falls to zero, and the needle springs back to the centre.

questions.stem: A student sweeps the wire left-right-left rhythmically through the gap. Describe the meter trace and connect it to the motion.
questions.modelAnswer: The needle kicks one way for each leftward sweep, swings through zero and kicks the other way for each rightward sweep, tracing a back-and-forth pattern that mirrors the wire's motion. The trace is alternating because the cutting direction alternates — the meter is effectively plotting the wire's velocity.

questions.stem: Why does a coil induce more voltage than a single wire in the same changing field?

options.explanation: Thickness is not the induction lever.

options.text: single wires cannot induce at all
options.explanation: They can — coils just add more.

options.text: every turn adds its own induced voltage
options.explanation: The turns' voltages sum along the coil.

options.text: the coil stores voltage for release later
options.explanation: Nothing is stored; induction is immediate.

questions.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil, then pulled back out at the same speed. The second kick is:

options.explanation: Same speed gives the same size; direction flips.
Leaving still changes the field through the coil.
Symmetric motion gives symmetric size.

options.text: the same size but the opposite direction
options.explanation: Exit reverses the field change, flipping the polarity.

questions.stem: Which change increases the induced voltage in a coil-and-magnet setup?

options.explanation: Speed is one of the three factors.
A weaker field reduces the voltage.
Fewer turns reduce the summed voltage.

options.text: holding the magnet perfectly still inside the coil
options.explanation: A steady field through the coil induces nothing.

questions.stem: A magnet sits motionless inside a large coil. Why does the meter read zero?

options.explanation: The circuit is complete; the physics gives zero.

options.text: the field through the coil is not changing
options.explanation: Induction needs a changing field or cutting.

options.text: the coil is too large to induce
options.explanation: Larger coils with more turns induce MORE.
The field exists — it just is not changing.

questions.stem: Two identical coils are threaded by the same changing field; one has 100 turns, the other 500. The 500-turn coil's induced voltage is:

options.explanation: Turn count is a size factor.
Same-direction turns add; they never cancel.
Voltage scales with the number of turns.
More turns induce more, not less.

questions.stem: State the effect on induced voltage of each of the three factors, increasing one at a time.
questions.modelAnswer: Faster movement, a stronger magnetic field and more turns each increase the induced voltage.

questions.stem: State the polarity relationship between a magnet entering and leaving a coil.
questions.modelAnswer: The induced voltage reverses: entering gives one polarity and leaving gives the opposite.

questions.stem: Explain why more turns on a coil give a larger induced voltage.
questions.modelAnswer: The changing field threads every turn of the coil identically, so each turn has its own induced voltage. The turns are connected in series along the coil, so the voltages add: double the turns doubles the total induced potential difference across the coil.

questions.stem: A generator demo uses a hand-cranked magnet spinning near a coil. Predict the meter trace as the crank turns steadily, and predict the change when the crank is turned twice as fast.
questions.modelAnswer: Steady cranking makes the field through the coil swing one way then the other each revolution, so the meter traces an alternating back-and-forth pattern in step with the crank. Twice the crank speed gives an alternating trace of the same shape but with twice the size and twice the frequency, because faster relative motion induces larger voltages more often.
